growth_story.headline: Barbados lost a decade after 2008, reset its debt in 2018 and rode tourism back, yet income per person is about where it was in 2005.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990, growth in income per person in Barbados has run in four eras: -0.1 percent a year in 1990–1997, 1.9 in 1998–2007, -2.2 in 2008–2015 and 1.5 in 2016–2025. The 1990s opened with heavy pressure on the currency and a sharp budget correction, and growth came back in the middle of the decade. Income per person peaked in 2008. The global financial crisis followed, and in early 2014 the IMF said the economy had still not recovered, with low growth, a high budget deficit and rising debt. In 2018 a new government restructured the public debt under its BERT plan, but income per person barely moved in 2016–2019, and the pandemic cut it by 17.5 percent in 2020. A tourism-led rebound followed, with growth of 15.9 percent in 2022 and slower gains since, which left income per person in 2025 6.5 percent below its 2008 peak and about where it first was in 2005.

threads.title: Tourism sets the rhythm
threads.text: Barbados earns its living mainly from tourism, so its growth rises and falls with the number of visitors and how long they stay. Recent gains came from more flights and a cricket world cup that drew visitors.

threads.title: A lost decade after 2008
threads.text: The global financial crisis left lasting damage: years later the economy had not recovered, and growth was low while the budget deficit and debt were high. The slump lasted beyond the crisis: in 2008–2019 the economy shrank in most years, jobs fell and the population declined.

since_last_year.text: Growth slowed in the first half of 2026. Visitors stayed for shorter periods and airlines flew fewer seats, though the number of arrivals held up. Business services and trade made up part of the gap. In mid-2026 the IMF approved a new precautionary arrangement to back the government's BERT 2026 plan.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe robust growth and a strong recovery since the 2018 reset, and in 2025 the authorities said activity had passed pre-pandemic levels. The data agree that the economy has rebounded, but income per person in 2025 is still 6.5 percent below its 2008 peak and about where it first was in 2005. The 1.5 percent average for 2016–2025 also leans on the bounce after the 2020 collapse: in 2016–2019, the years of the debt reset, income per person barely grew.
